The most recent statements, for the 2024 financial year, were approved on 30 June 2025 and widely reported, including disclosure of a loss and a restatement of the prior year's results following an accounting anomaly. Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: No Mozambique-specific evidence found for explicit refugee/migrant access provisions in KYC/mobile money regulations or programs (searches included “refugee migrant mobile money Mozambique KYC”).
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced Mozambique-specific evidence, so this row moved from the fast path to a full review. A World Bank report (2023) on Mozambique's government-to-person payments describes Banco de Moçambique 'comfort letters' permitting National Institute of Social Action (INAS) beneficiary cards to satisfy KYC requirements for opening mobile-money accounts, easing access for under-documented and internally displaced beneficiaries. An NRC cash-for-protection pilot report for internally displaced persons in Cabo Delgado (2022) documents M-Pesa transfers delivered to displaced beneficiaries via SMS voucher without requiring a pre-existing registered account. No evidence of a comprehensive legal framework specifically recognising refugee, asylum-seeker or migrant documentation for KYC purposes was found; standard KYC under Decree 53/2023 requires a national identity document or passport. Score revised from 0/Unknown to 2/Partial, reflecting documented but limited practical access pathways for under-documented and displaced populations rather than a comprehensive framework.
revised_comments: Mozambique has no dedicated legal framework granting refugees, asylum seekers or migrants explicit rights to open digital payment accounts, and standard know-your-customer rules require a national identity document or passport. In practice, partial pathways exist for under-documented and displaced populations: the central bank has issued 'comfort letters' allowing National Institute of Social Action (INAS) beneficiary cards to satisfy KYC requirements for mobile-money accounts used for government-to-person payments, and humanitarian cash-transfer programmes, such as the Norwegian Refugee Council's cash-for-protection project for internally displaced persons in Cabo Delgado, have distributed M-Pesa mobile money to recipients without an existing registered account via redeemable SMS vouchers.
